speaker: lisahobbs
text: May it please the Court. The Texas Antiquities Code is a little-known and unique statute that the legislature adopted to protect and preserve Texas' archaeological heritage. How did the legislature decide to do this? Well, they made every single Texan a steward of our natural resources. Not just a single state agency, not a governmental task force, but literally every single one of us stewards of those natural resources. Second, the legislature also empowered each Texan with the right to seek protection of those assets in our court system. And I want to start there with the legislative intent and the Antiquities Code itself, because understanding this unique aspect of the Antiquities Code will lead this court to conclude that the trial court was correct to deny the city's plea to the jurisdiction, but irrational and wrong in denying Dr. Grossman's application for temporary injunction. Specific to this appeal, the Antiquities Code declares in Section 191.002 that it is the policy of the state of Texas that Native American campsite and habitation sites should be located, protected, and preserved. Those are the precise words of the statute. And that's really why we're here. In October of 2018, new and groundbreaking research indicated the existence of a Mescalero Apache peace camp, if you will, that existed on this record indisputably within Duranguito. This is significant research, and I think this is really important for you to understand, because of the Mescalero Apache lifestyle. See, this group of Indians was largely nomadic. That's my word. I think our experts use the word hunters and gatherers, but they moved around a lot. They didn't build pueblos or trade pottery for their livelihood, as many tribes in the area may have done in this era. To have a camp where thousands of them existed for an extended period of time makes Santiago's research and the book that was published on October 28th significant and an opportunity to study this particular tribe in a way that we have not really been able to do in the Southwest region. The Mescalero Apache's nomadic lifestyle also is kind of the heart of what is wrong with the city's scope of work that Mr. Mangrum did, and why Dr. Grossman has filed a lawsuit to say that it is wholly inadequate to locate, protect, and preserve the Mescalero Apache remains as is required under the Antiquities Code. Now, I'm certain that Mr. Osborne will get up here and say that the scope of work already takes into account Native American remains, and it does reference them, but it does not take into account this particular type of Native American remains, and that is really the heart of this lawsuit. And if the trial court failed to appreciate that after two days of testimony and argument in this case, then that was an abuse of discretion. And in fact, I would posit that there were a few failures by the trial court in this case, and I would want to start with appreciating my burden here. It is not easy to get an appellate court to say that a trial court abused its discretion in failing to issue an injunction. But I think I can give you three reasons why the trial court in this particular case abused its discretion in not enjoining the city from starting its project without having an adequate scope of review before the commission. And here's what I would say about that. First, to the extent that the trial court denied the temporary injunction based on a failure to state a viable claim, I believe that the trial court applied too high of a standard. We have a viable claim. We have set forth enough evidence to show a probable right to recovery on those claims. Second, to the extent that the T.I., the denial of the T.I. was based on lack of proof of irreparable injury, we believe that would be both legally wrong, inconsistent with Texas's jurisprudence on what we would need to show, and inconsistent with the factual record that we presented to the trial court at the hearing.

speaker: lisahobbs
text: That's a good question, Your Honor, and you're getting to the heart of what this case is about. But if you look at Dr. Carmichael's testimony about the problems that he has with the scope of work, which is truly the basis of this lawsuit, he finds three problems with the scope of work, none of which were really completely defended. There is some conflicting evidence on it, but the three problems that he faults the Mangum scope of work with are, first of all, the scope of work does not have a systematic way for discovering this particular type of Indian remains. It's a very European focus, so you'll get a lot of European remains and things like that, but to get to these sort of low visibility remains, his scope of work doesn't have just a systematic way to do it. And then the scope of work, the plan in the current scope of work is it's a mechanical excavation of these things. And one of the first things they're going to do is to do some ground penetrating radar so that they can find remains underneath the surface. And again, that's great for finding European remains, that's great for finding even possibly like pottery and things like that, Native American remains that are different than the kinds of remains that you would find with this type of tribe. But the radar penetration will not find these low visibility remains, according to Dr. Carmichael and the testimony that we presented to the trial court. And then finally, one of the things that's definitely not addressed by Mr. Mangum in any way, shape, or form is the scope of work's decision to use a quarter inch screen to, when you pull out the remains, it's screened through certain sizes of instruments. And the scope of work anticipates using a quarter screen mesh in order to find those remains. But Dr. Carmichael has noted his opinion that that would be insufficient to find low visibility remains. He did a study with his students on a particular site, and they found that 90% of the remains were not found using a quarter inch mesh, and they would be found if you included it, if you use a eighth of an inch mesh like Dr. Carmichael recommends.

speaker: jeffalley
text: And it really raises my core question, which is, if these issues are raised to the THC, which is an agency that I would think has expertise in these areas, at least far more expertise than I have, why wouldn't we defer to them, maybe almost like a Chevron or our deference?

speaker: lisahobbs
text: Well, I mean, well, let me just say for Chevron purposes, it wouldn't come into play because this isn't a lawsuit from an actual act by the agency. But, you know, it goes back to my opening, Chief, and it's just, the Antiquities Code is unique. No one doubts that the THC had the authority to require the city to redo their scope of work based on this new research that was not at all, no one knew about it when the city first applied for their permit. But to say that they have authority, there's nothing in the Antiquities Code or in their enabling statute that gives them the exclusive authority, and in fact, as I mentioned in my opening, the Antiquities Code is unique in that it does make us all stewards of our archaeological heritage. It makes me a steward, Dr. Grossman a steward, you a steward, you know, the trial court a steward, and that's its intent, is these are precious assets, and we all have a role in protecting them, and the Antiquities Code itself gives us all that, not only obligation, but the ability to make sure that they're protected. One of the things going back to just the standard on why I believe that there is an abuse of discretion in this case is, to my third point, I listed, number one, the trial court either got the standard wrong on what we needed to show to show probable right to relief and a successful claim, two, on irreparable injury, and then the third is that the trial court abused its discretion in failing to balance the equities of this case, and the case that we cited in our brief that is a good case is the Seaborg-Jackson case out of Dallas from 1988, and it recognizes that a trial court who doesn't do, I mean, an injunction, a temporary injunction or final injunction, those are equitable remedies, and because they're equitable remedies, they require a balancing of the equities, and in Seaborg-Jackson, the Dallas court did find that a trial court abused its discretion in not considering the equities of this case, and that goes to the overarching question for this court is, did Dr. Grossman do enough to show that his claims are likely to succeed on the merits, enough to show that we should get a trial on the merits? This was a very short and rushed discovery on these claims. We believe we can dive into this more deeply and have a trial on the merits, and the question right now is, should we keep the status quo right now, like where the city is right now, where we are right now, so that we have an opportunity to go to the trial on the merits? And the balance of equities in this case certainly suggests that we should. If we start, commence this project in any way, even with the demolition of the buildings, the testimony at trial indicates that we could disturb these archaeological remains. Dr. Mangum, I mean, Mr. Mangum, says so in his scope of work. He says that it could have been, we could unintentionally disturb these remains. Dr. Grossman, who has an archaeological background, says that, yes, demolishing buildings with this big equipment can disturb the soil underneath it enough to, you know, lose these remains of the Mescalero Apaches. And Dr. Carmichael said that if Mr. Mangum is correct about the depth of these Mescalero Apache remains, then yes, using huge equipment to demolish these buildings could in fact put the archaeological remains underneath the soil at risk.

speaker: lisahobbs

The city has its own obligation to protect and preserve the Mescalero Apache remains. text: Please report and counsel. Let me just address a couple of the issues that were raised in your questioning and discussion with me. So I would like to begin by consideration of the big picture. Here the city followed the antiquities code. It was told to apply for a permit for an archaeology survey. It did that. It hired more a respected archaeology firm who's done had numerous dealings with the THC and worked with them on numerous surveys around the state. Prepared a research design, prepared a scope of work, submitted it to the THC. The THC reviewed it. They have archaeologists on staff, including the state archaeologists, the highest archaeologist in the state. They reviewed it and required revisions. Moore went back and made those revisions, submitted a revised scope of work, and that's what the THC has approved. And then the other important thing is to keep in mind the big picture here in terms of the survey. We are looking for Native American artifacts, but not only Native American artifacts. We're looking at artifacts from all periods of time. Ms. Hobbs again misstated. She did it in her brief and said that Mangum City was only going to go two feet. That was a theoretical example he gave to doing a, if you're going to build a road, you might go two or three feet down. speaker: markosborn
text: With all respect, due to us as lawyers and judges, the simple answer is no. The court does not have the jurisdiction to review the decision of the THC. It's a discretionary matter left to the THC to decide. And what Ms. Hobbs left out of that description of this section of the statute that is the basis for Dr. Grossman's claim, which is 191.173A of the Antiquities Code, it permits suits by citizens to enjoin threatened or violations or threatened violations of the Antiquities Code, which is Chapter 191 of the Texas Natural Resources Code. But what it does not allow, because it would have to expressly state it, is a suit against the state or a subdivision of the state. There's no waiver of governmental immunity.

speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: Okay, so let me stop you right there for a minute. speaker: markosborn
text: I'm sorry, but do you mean a governmental actor? Yes. A city on its own land?

speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: Yes.

speaker: markosborn

speaker: yvonnerodriguez
text: Yeah, don't misunderstand me. Don't mistake me, Mr. Osborne. I fully understand the idea of sovereign immunity. It's just difficult for me to envision that this Texas Antiquities Act is only to apply to private landowners, because then it doesn't further the purpose of the act, which is to protect those antiquities. It doesn't seem rational to me.

speaker: markosborn
text: Here's the test. So there's no question there's not an express waiver of sovereign immunity. That right was not present in the statute. Grossman's argument is that the court should imply it. The test for implying a waiver of immunity is, is the statute meaningless without it? Here, and we're talking about the entire Antiquities Code, all of Chapter 191. Chapter 191 prohibits the removal, altering, damaging, or excavating without a permit or in violation of a permit, shipwrecks and their contents, buried treasure, historical artifacts on state land, and that would be by someone going on to state land to do it, a private party. The statute also prohibits facing artifacts, monuments, historical structures, and Native American paintings and carvings. All of those prohibitions could be violated by private actors. And so the statute has meaning because it allows any citizen of the state of Texas to go in if someone is doing that and get an injunction to prohibit those violations. Thus the statute has meaning. What Grossman's argument really is, is that the statute will have broader application if you imply a waiver. But that's not the law, that's not the test. And the reason is, if that were the test, you would always imply a waiver. Because every statute will have broader application if you have a waiver of sovereign immunity. Counsel?
